auditFix.issue: 몰다 means to drive (a car, a herd of animals), not to ride a bicycle. The standard Korean collocation for bicycles is 자전거를 타다. 자전거를 몰다 is unnatural and would strike native speakers as wrong; 몰다 only fits motorized vehicles like 차/오토바이 or animals being driven (소떼를 몰다).

entries.gloss: My hands are shaking from the cold.

auditFix.issue: The headword is 떨다 (transitive: to shake something deliberately), but the sentence uses the intransitive/passive form 떨리다 (떨려요). 떨다 takes an object (다리를 떨다 = to shake one's leg), whereas involuntary trembling from cold uses 떨리다 (손이 떨리다). The example illustrates the wrong lemma; learners studying 떨다 will incorrectly internalize 떨려요 as its conjugation. Replace with a 떨다 example such as '아이가 다리를 떨고 있어요' or change the headword to 떨리다.

auditFix.issue: The standard term for the body of traffic rules drivers/pedestrians follow is 교통 법규 or 교통 규칙 (or the formal statute name 도로교통법, no internal space). 교통 법 (with a space, just '법') is unidiomatic — 법 alone is the abstract noun 'law' and pairs with major bodies of law (헌법, 형법) rather than with everyday compliance. auditFix.issue: Wrong locative particle. Korean uses 에서 (not 에) to mark the location where an action takes place; 에 only marks static existence/destination. 굽다 (to bake) is an action verb, so it must be 오븐에서 빵을 구워요. 'Bread is in the oven' would be 빵이 오븐에 있어요, but for the act of baking, 에서 is required.

entries.korean: 엄마가 여행길에 먹을 밥을 짓고 계세요.
entries.gloss: Mom is cooking rice to eat on the journey.

auditFix.issue: Gloss/Korean mismatch. The Korean subject is 어머니 (mother), but the English gloss still says 'The farmer is cooking rice.' This is leftover stale text from the prior auditFix that swapped 농부 → 어머니 to better match 밥을 짓다 collocation but did not update the gloss. Gloss must read 'Mother is cooking rice.'

priorAuditFix.issue: Grammatical but pragmatically odd. 밥을 짓다 is correct Korean (HiNative confirms it as the standard, slightly literary expression for cooking rice). However, a 농부 (farmer) prototypically '농사를 짓다' (does farming), not '밥을 짓다' in their professional capacity. Native speakers would naturally pair 밥을 짓다 with 어머니/할머니. Switching to 어머니 keeps the headword 짓다 with its most idiomatic collocation and removes the cognitive friction.

auditFix.issue: Korean sentence is grammatical and idiomatic — 쌀(uncooked rice) + 로(instrumental) + 밥을 짓다(cook rice/make a meal) is the canonical collocation. However, the English gloss 'Mother cooks rice from grains' collapses the very 쌀(uncooked)/밥(cooked) distinction the example sentence exists to teach: a learner cannot tell which Korean word is the headword 쌀, and 'grains' is an unidiomatic stand-in for 'uncooked rice'. Re-gloss to preserve the contrast.

auditFix.issue: 이렇다 is overwhelmingly used either attributively (이런 + noun) or in its 반말/요체 contracted forms (이래/이래요). Standalone 날씨가 이렇네요 is grammatical only as a deictic comment requiring a shared visible referent (gesturing at bad weather), which a flashcard cannot supply. As a textbook sentence it reads as incomplete. Reframing with 이렇다 inside a 이런 ~ 날씨 attributive structure makes the headword's usage pattern clearer and is unambiguously well-formed in isolation.

auditFix.issue: The structure '이제 그만 + V' means 'stop V-ing now', so '이제 그만 쉴까요?' naturally reads as 'Shall we stop resting now?' (i.e., go back to working) — the opposite of the intended gloss 'Shall we stop now and rest?'. To express 'stop and rest', the standard form is '이제 그만하고 쉴까요?' or '이제 (일은) 그만하고 좀 쉴까요?'.

auditFix.issue: Spacing error. 벚 is a bound morpheme that cannot stand alone; 벚꽃 is the established word for cherry blossom. The sentence should be either 벚꽃잎이... or 벚꽃 잎이... — 벚 꽃잎 splits the wrong morpheme boundary.

auditFix.issue: 불리다 ('to be called/named') normally takes a noun complement via -(이)라고 불리다 ('is called X-name'), e.g. '천재라고 불려요'. Pairing it with the descriptive clause 친절하다고 ('that he is kind') is unnatural; for being known/described as having a quality, 알려져 있다 or 평가받다 is the right verb.

auditFix.issue: Confirmed parse ambiguity: 길이 can be tokenized either as 길+이 (subject-marked 'road') or as 길이 (the noun 'length'). Native readers may briefly garden-path. Korean parsing literature (Eojoel ambiguity) documents this exact class of segmentation problem. Dropping the redundant subject particle (양쪽 길 모두 ...) eliminates the ambiguity and matches the more natural collocation.
